abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Antimicrobial resistance poses a significant challenge to conventional antibiotics, underscoring the urgent need for alternative therapeutic strategies. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have emerged as promising candidates due to their broad-spectrum antibacterial activity and distinct mechanisms of action. This study presents ANIA, a deep learning framework developed to predict the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values of AMPs against three clinically significant bacteria: Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. ANIA leverages Chaos Game Representation (CGR) to transform AMP sequences into frequency-based image features, which are subsequently processed through a hybrid architecture comprising stacked Inception modules, a Transformer encoder, and a regression head. This integrative architecture enables ANIA to capture both local motif-based features and global contextual patterns embedded within AMP sequences. In benchmarking experiments, ANIA achieved notably superior performance compared to existing tools, including ESKAPEE-Pred, AMPActiPred, and esAMPMIC, achieving higher correlation coefficients and lower predictive errors across all bacteria targets, with the most pronounced improvement observed for P. aeruginosa, a pathogen renowned for its multidrug resistance. Specifically, ANIA achieved PCCs of 0.75–0.79 and MSEs of 0.23–0.26 across all species. Furthermore, motif-based interpretability analyses combining Grad-CAM visualizations, correlation heatmaps, motif frequency distributions, and hydrophobicity profiling revealed biologically meaningful subregions within the CGR matrix that are plausibly associated with antimicrobial efficacy. In conclusion, this study develops ANIA as a robust predictive tool for MIC estimation, offering valuable insights into the design of effective antimicrobial agents and contributing to the fight against antimicrobial resistance. A user-friendly web server for ANIA is available at https://biomics.lab.nycu.edu.tw/ANIA/.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The overuse of antibiotics has precipitated a global health crisis, as antibiotic-resistant bacteria increasingly compromise the efficacy of conventional therapies [1, 2]. Antibiotic resistance, confirmed as a major threat, causes millions of deaths annually [3]. Among the most concerning are the ESKAPE pathogens, including Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), Escherichia coli (E. coli), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa), which are characterized by their multidrug resistance and frequent association with severe healthcare-related infections such as pneumonia and bacteremia [4, 5]. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have emerged as promising therapeutic candidates, demonstrating rapid bactericidal activity and effectiveness against resistant strains [6]. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), a key metric for evaluating AMP potency, plays a crucial role in guiding treatment strategies. However, conventional MIC determination remains labor-intensive and time-consuming, thus motivating the development of efficient computational prediction methods [7].

Machine learning has advanced AMP analysis, initially focusing on classification. Classifiers, such as AntiBP and AMPScanner, utilized algorithms to identify antibacterial peptides, but provided only binary outputs [8–15]. Subsequently, to address this limitation, a new class of models was developed to estimate MIC values directly. Xiao et al. employed pseudo-amino acid composition and Gaussian kernel regression to model AMP activity against E. coli [16], while Yan et al. applied a multi-branch convolutional neural network (CNN) with attention mechanisms, trained on data from the DBAASP database [17]. More recently, ensemble learning has been applied to improve generalization across species. For instance, Chung et al. developed an ensemble deep learning model for MIC regression across multiple pathogens [18], and AMPActiPred implemented a three-stage deep forest framework capable of both AMP identification and MIC prediction [19]. Additionally, ESKAPEE-MICpred incorporated genomic and language model features to capture pathogen-specific AMP interactions [20]. Despite these advances, most existing models remain limited in their ability to capture spatial dependencies within AMP sequences, as traditional encoding schemes may not fully preserve the spatial patterns necessary for accurate MIC prediction [21].

Parallel innovations in AI have further expanded the possibilities for AMP discovery and optimization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs), such as the feedback-based design framework by Zervou et al., have been used to synthesize novel peptides with enhanced antimicrobial properties [22]. Transformer-based architectures like ProtTrans have demonstrated strong performance in capturing long-range sequence dependencies relevant to antimicrobial activity [23]. Reinforcement learning has also shown promise, as demonstrated by Wang et al., who developed an optimization framework that iteratively refines AMP sequences to balance potency and toxicity [24]. Moreover, hybrid models that integrate empirical screening data with deep learning architectures, such as combinations of CNNs and recurrent neural networks [14], reflect a growing trend toward more comprehensive modeling of AMP functionality. Collectively, these strategies underscore the transformative potential of AI-driven methodologies in advancing both AMP prediction and rational design [25–27].

Despite recent progress in computational approaches, critical challenges remain in accurately predicting AMP activity and MIC values. Many traditional models rely primarily on sequence-derived features, such as pseudo-amino acid composition, which often fail to capture spatial patterns essential for modeling AMP–bacteria interactions [21]. In addition, numerous existing frameworks lack integration of physicochemical properties that are vital to AMP function, thereby limiting predictive accuracy across diverse bacterial species [28]. Practical application is further hindered by the high synthesis cost and molecular complexity of AMPs, reinforcing the need for more efficient and informative predictive strategies [6].

To address these limitations, we propose a novel computational pipeline that leverages Chaos Game Representation (CGR) encoding to convert AMP sequences into image-based frequency matrices, effectively preserving the spatial distribution of sequence motifs [29, 30]. This encoding facilitates the application of computer vision methods, enabling the model to capture both local sequential features and global structural patterns [31]. Building on this foundation, we developed ANIA, a deep learning framework designed to predict MIC values of AMPs against three clinically relevant pathogens: S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa [31, 32]. Unlike conventional binary classifiers, ANIA adopts a regression-based strategy to estimate MIC values as continuous outcomes, enabling fine-grained assessments of antimicrobial activity [7].

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: An overview of the ANIA workflow is provided in Fig. 1, and the web server (https://biomics.lab.nycu.edu.tw/ANIA/) offers a publicly accessible platform for practical application. Specifically, Figs 1A–F illustrates the complete workflow: (A) dataset collection and preprocessing, (B) CGR-based encoding and FCGR generation, (C) model architecture integrating Inception and Transformer modules, (D) training and validation procedures, (E) interpretability and feature attribution analyses, and (F) deployment of the ANIA web interface.

caption.p: Workflow of the ANIA-based MIC prediction system. (A) Dataset collection and preprocessing. Antimicrobial peptide sequences and corresponding MIC values targeting E. coli, S. aureus, and P. aeruginosa were curated from public databases (DBAASP, dbAMP, DRAMP). (B) Image feature extraction using CGR and frequency matrix transformation. (C) Model construction using an inception-attention network with 5-fold cross-validation and evaluation on an independent test set. (D) Performance comparison with conventional machine learning methods and existing AMP prediction tools. (E) Feature-level explainability analysis based on FCGR-derived spatial patterns and physicochemical property mapping. (F) Web server development for user interaction, FASTA input submission, prediction display, and CSV export.

graphic.alt-text: Diagram illustrating a workflow for data processing, model training, evaluation, interpretation, and web-based prediction.

sec.title: Data sources and preparation
sec.p: AMP sequences targeting S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa were curated from DBAASP [33], dbAMP [34], and DRAMP [35]. These repositories provided validated sequences and MIC values, supporting predictive modeling. The ESKAPE pathogens were selected for their multidrug resistance and clinical relevance [5]. The dataset comprised 8283, 7582, and 5621 sequences for S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa, respectively, partitioned into 4:1 training and test sets with 5-fold cross-validation. Detailed preprocessing steps are provided in Supplementary Note 1.1. The number of AMP sequences allocated to the training and test sets for each bacterial species is summarized in Supplementary Table S1.

sec.title: CGR encoding for AMP sequence representation
sec.p: To transform AMP sequences into a format compatible with deep learning models designed for image-based data, we employed CGR encoding to convert each sequence into a two-dimensional frequency matrix. CGR is a mathematical technique based on iterated function systems, which maps sequential data into a fractal representation within a unit square, effectively preserving the spatial distribution of sequence motifs [29]. This representation has been widely recognized as a robust feature encoding strategy for biological sequences, including DNA, RNA, and proteins, and has facilitated the application of computer vision-based methods in various prediction tasks [30, 31, 36, 37]. In our study, this encoding enables the transformation of AMP sequences into image-like representations suitable for MIC regression modeling.
These coordinates were assigned to the 20 amino acids in alphabetical order (A, C, D, …, Y), ensuring a balanced and symmetrical distribution across the unit square.

caption.p: Overview of CGR encoding and the ANIA model architecture. (A) Step-by-step example of applying CGR on a AMP sequence (length = 54). The peptide sequence is fragmented into overlapping sliding 3-mers, which are sequentially mapped onto 2D CGR space. Intermediate steps of the CGR trajectory are shown at selected position index (i), demonstrating how sequence order and motif information are encoded into a spatial frequency distribution (FCGR). (B) Motif-level visualization on FCGR matrix generated from the example sequence, where each pixel represents the normalized frequency of a specific 3-mer pattern within the predefined CGR grid. Representative sub-regions are enlarged to illustrate how distinct amino-acid combinations contribute to localized frequency intensities. (C) The overall framework of ANIA, comprising stacked Inception modules, a Transformer encoder, and a regression head for MIC prediction. (D) Internal configuration of the Inception module, with four parallel branches for extracting multi-scale sequence features.

graphic.alt-text: Diagram illustrating CGR-based sequence encoding and the overall architecture of the ANIA prediction model.

sec.p: Supplementary Figs S1A–C display the FCGR representations of AMP sequences targeting S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa, respectively. Within each species, discernible differences emerged between sequences associated with low and high MIC values. For example, sequences with lower MIC values exhibited elevated motif frequencies in specific grid regions, suggesting potential hotspots linked to antimicrobial activity. These visual patterns provide preliminary insights into sequence-function relationships and are particularly informative for the downstream regression task of MIC prediction.

The FCGR matrix serves as an image-based representation of the AMP sequence, capturing the spatial distribution of sequence motifs that are critical for MIC estimation. This format is well-suited for computer vision-based deep learning models, enabling them to leverage structured motif frequency patterns to enhance predictive accuracy. Moreover, the FCGR representation facilitates interpretability by allowing visual analysis of sequence motif distributions, as demonstrated in our feature interpretation experiments.

sec.title: ANIA model architecture
sec.p: Predicting MIC values from FCGR representations requires the model to capture both localized motif patterns, which reflect physicochemical residue interactions, and global spatial dependencies, which describe the overall organization of functional regions within the peptide map. To meet these dual requirements, ANIA was designed as a hybrid architecture that combines convolutional and attention-based mechanisms. Specifically, ANIA integrates two stacked Inception modules to extract multi-scale local motifs. In this study, two Inception modules were stacked sequentially, providing an optimal balance between predictive performance, architectural complexity, and computational efficiency based on empirical evaluation (see Supplementary Table S3). The extracted features are subsequently processed by a Transformer encoder that models long-range dependencies across the FCGR representation. A final regression head is employed to estimate MIC values. This hybrid design leverages the complementary strengths of convolutional feature extraction and attention-driven contextual learning, enabling the model to jointly learn fine-grained spatial features and global dependency patterns from image-based peptide representations. The overall architecture of ANIA is illustrated in Fig. 2C. The model was implemented in Python using the PyTorch framework and trained on an NVIDIA GPU platform.

The encoder output is globally pooled and passed through a three-layer fully connected regression head with a hidden dimension of 64 and dropout rates ranging from 0.4 to 0.6. This head applies dropout-based regularization and produces a scalar output representing the predicted MIC value.

The model’s hyperparameters were selected to balance architectural complexity and predictive performance. Instead of relying on fixed-scale filters, the Inception modules incorporate multiple kernel sizes and learnable branch weights to adaptively extract sequence features across varying receptive fields. Similarly, the Transformer encoder, configured with one layer and two attention heads, enables the model to capture long-range dependencies across embedded spatial features. A complete specification of the ANIA architecture—including kernel dimensions, channel sizes, number of layers, activation functions, and pooling strategies—is provided in Supplementary Table S4. Model training was performed using the Adam optimizer with Mean Squared Error loss and early stopping based on validation loss. Training convergence was consistently achieved within ~40–50 epochs across folds, indicating stable optimization behavior and reliable generalization.

sec.title: Evaluation metrics
Distributional analysis of AMP sequence length and log MIC distribution across targeted bacteria
sec.p: Log-transformed MIC values displayed distinct species-specific patterns (Fig. 3A). S. aureus showed a relatively symmetric distribution, while E. coli and P. aeruginosa exhibited broader spreads with mild skewness toward higher MIC values. These differences reflect interspecies variability in AMP susceptibility and emphasize the need for pathogen-specific modeling strategies. As shown in Fig. 3B, a consistent negative correlation was observed between sequence length and log MIC across all species, indicating that longer AMPs tend to exhibit stronger antimicrobial activity. Detailed descriptions of distributional characteristics and regression parameters are provided in Supplementary Note 1.4.

caption.p: (A) Distributions of log MIC values for AMP sequences targeting S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa. (B) Relationship between AMP sequence length and log MIC values across species, with fitted linear trend lines.

graphic.alt-text: Plots illustrating the distribution of log MIC values and the relationship between peptide length and antimicrobial activity across different bacteria.

sec.title: Performance of machine learning models with iFeature encoding
sec.p: To establish a baseline for MIC prediction, we evaluated conventional machine learning models trained on iFeature-derived descriptors [42], comprising physicochemical, structural, and compositional features (Supplementary Table S5). The models comprised linear regressors (Linear Regression [43], Lasso [44], Ridge [45], Elastic Net [46]), tree-based ensembles (Random Forest, RF [47], Gradient Boosting [48], XGBoost [49]), and a kernel-based method (Support Vector Machine, SVM [50]). Model performance was evaluated on independent test sets for S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa (Table 1). Gradient Boosting achieved the highest predictive performance, with the strongest PCC and explained variance across species. RF and XGBoost also performed robustly, while linear models showed reduced accuracy, particularly for P. aeruginosa. SVM exhibited intermediate results. Notably, E. coli showed the best overall results, possibly due to its larger dataset and stronger sequence length–MIC association.

caption.p: Evaluation of machine learning models for MIC prediction using iFeature-derived features on the independent test set.

sec.p: While these results highlight the utility of traditional machine learning with sequence-derived descriptors, the moderate predictive accuracy underscores limitations in capturing complex, non-linear determinants of antimicrobial activity. These findings provide a reference point for evaluating CGR-based feature representations and the ANIA deep learning framework, which are specifically designed to capture spatial and contextual patterns beyond the reach of conventional models.

sec.title: Performance of machine learning models with CGR encoding
sec.p: To assess the predictive utility of CGR-based features independently of deep learning architectures, we re-evaluated the previously tested machine learning algorithms using CGR encoding, which transforms AMP sequences into frequency-based image representations. Model performance on independent test sets for S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa is summarized in Table 2. Across species, predictive accuracy varied with both the choice of algorithm and target bacterium. SVM achieved the best results, though overall performance was lower than with iFeature-derived descriptors. Although CGR encodes spatial sequence patterns absent in conventional descriptors, its combination with traditional models did not improve predictive accuracy.

caption.p: Evaluation of machine learning models for MIC prediction using CGR-encoded features on the independent test set.

sec.p: This limitation arises from a mismatch between CGR’s structured, hierarchical information and the flat data assumptions of tree-based or kernel-based models. These results underscore the need for deep learning frameworks—such as ANIA—that are specifically designed to process CGR matrices and capture contextual biological features.

sec.title: Performance of the ANIA model
sec.p: To overcome the limitations of traditional machine learning models in leveraging CGR-encoded features, we evaluated the proposed ANIA deep learning model, which is specifically designed to extract and integrate the spatial and contextual information embedded in CGR representations. Figure 4A summarizes the comparative performance of ANIA versus the best-performing traditional model —Gradient Boosting for iFeature-derived descriptors and SVM for FCGR-based features—across S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa. The full numerical results are available in Supplementary Table S6. Across all three bacterial species, ANIA consistently outperformed both traditional models on every performance metric. For instance, on S. aureus, using FCGR features, ANIA reduced the MAE from 0.4720 (SVM) to 0.3899 and increased the PCC from 0.6058 to 0.7518. A similar trend was observed for E. coli, with MAE reduced from 0.4557 to 0.3839 and PCC improved from 0.6640 to 0.7923. Notably, for P. aeruginosa, where traditional models demonstrated relatively poor predictive power, ANIA achieved a substantial performance gain, improving MAE from 0.4442 to 0.3643 and boosting PCC from 0.6256 to 0.7822.

caption.p: Performance evaluation of ANIA for AMP MIC prediction. (A) Bar chart comparing ANIA versus gradient boosting using iFeature and FCGR encodings across MAE, MSE, R2, PCC, and Spearman for S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa. (B) Scatter plots of predicted versus actual log MIC values by ANIA for each bacterium, showing regression accuracy. (C) Bar chart comparing ANIA with ESKAPEE-MICpred, esAMPMIC, and AMPActiPred across MAE, MSE, R2, PCC, and Spearman on an independent test set for the same bacteria. Red stars indicate metrics where ANIA achieved the best performance.

graphic.alt-text: Charts and scatter plots illustrating the prediction performance of different models for MIC estimation across multiple bacterial species.

sec.p: These results underscore ANIA’s strength in capturing the spatially structured patterns within CGR-based representations—patterns that conventional models fail to exploit effectively. The model’s superior and consistent performance across all bacterial species highlights its robustness and affirms its potential as a powerful predictive framework for MIC estimation in antimicrobial peptide research. Figure 4B further visualizes the predicted versus actual MIC values obtained by ANIA for each bacterial species, demonstrating close alignment with experimental values and validating the reliability of the model’s regression predictions.

sec.title: Interpretability analysis and feature attribution visualization

caption.p: Motif-level interpretability analysis of the FCGR matrix for MIC prediction using E. coli as a representative example. (A) Motif-level composition map displaying the most representative 3-mer in each FCGR cell, providing a fine-grained overview of local sequence patterns. (B) Grad-CAM visualization of the ANIA model’s attention across the FCGR matrix, highlighting the upper-central and lower-left subregions most critical for MIC prediction. (C) Pearson correlation heatmap between individual FCGR cells and predicted log MIC values, confirming the statistical relevance of the highlighted subregions. (D) Differential motif frequency map showing occurrence differences of FCGR cell intensities between high-activity (low log MIC) and low-activity (high log MIC) peptides. (E) Heatmap of cell-wise weighted average hydrophobicity (ARGP820101 index) derived from 3-mer frequency analysis, illustrating hydrophobicity shifts between high-and low-activity groups. Orange and green boxes denote spatial zones consistently identified as the most prominent across multiple analyses.

graphic.alt-text: Motif maps and heatmaps illustrating FCGR-based patterns and interpretability analyses for antimicrobial peptide MIC prediction.

sec.p: Using E. coli as a representative example, we first examined the local sequence composition underlying each pixel to determine the types of 3-mer motifs that were encoded within the FCGR space. Because each pixel typically aggregates multiple 3-mers, Fig. 5A displays the most representative motif in each pixel, providing a fine-grained map of motif distribution across the grid. We then analyzed the model’s Grad-CAM attention map (Fig. 5B) to identify the pixels receiving the strongest activations during prediction. These attention-focused regions were enriched with recurring motif families characterized by cationic–hydrophobic combinations (e.g. RRI, KSI, KVA, KAI), short alanine- and leucine-dominated nonpolar fragments (e.g. LLS, KSA, LSA), and mixed polar–hydrophobic triplets containing aromatic or bulky residues (e.g. WWR, CYR, GVA). Collectively, these findings suggest that the ANIA model focuses on composite sequence–structure features shaped by the balance between cationic–hydrophobic enrichment and localized flexibility.

To further interpret the model’s focus regions, we highlighted two major subregions—colored in orange and green in Fig. 5B—that exhibited the strongest Grad-CAM activations in E. coli. We next examined the statistical association between these spatial patterns and predicted MIC values. A cell-wise Pearson correlation analysis (Fig. 5C) revealed that the attention-focused subregions displayed moderately strong negative correlations with predicted log MIC values, indicating that higher motif frequency in these areas tended to drive the model toward predicting higher antimicrobial potency.

To assess whether these correlations were reflected at the sequence level, we compared the FCGR intensity distributions between high-activity and low-activity peptides (Fig. 5D). The resulting difference map showed that the same attention-highlighted regions were preferentially enriched in high-activity peptides, whereas low-activity peptides exhibited more diffuse or depleted signal patterns. This correspondence between model attention and predicted activity grouping suggests that the ANIA model supports its decisions on spatially localized motif clusters that it internally associates with stronger activity.

Finally, we evaluated the physicochemical properties underlying these spatial motifs by computing cell-wise weighted average hydrophobicity using the ARGP820101 index (Fig. 5E) [51]. The attention-focused regions exhibited higher hydrophobicity values in high-activity peptides, consistent with prior experimental findings that greater hydrophobicity enhances peptide–membrane interactions and antimicrobial efficacy [28,52,53]. Cross-species comparison of attention-weighted motif distributions consistently supported these compositional trends across E. coli, P. aeruginosa, and S. aureus (see Supplementary Note 1.5).

Taken together, this integrative analysis identifies spatially coherent subregions within the FCGR matrix that exert a strong influence on the prediction of antimicrobial potency. By integrating spatial localization, correlation structure, and physicochemical context, our interpretability analysis reveals how ANIA internally associates specific motif compositions with high predicted activity, thereby clarifying the model’s decision basis. These insights not only enhance the transparency of the prediction process but also provide a foundation for rational AMP design guided by model-interpretable sequence features.

sec.title: Comparison with existing tools
sec.p: To further evaluate the predictive capability of the ANIA model, we conducted a comparative analysis against three established MIC prediction tools: ESKAPEE-Pred [20], esAMPMIC [18], and AMPActiPred [19]. These models were selected based on their relevance to AMP MIC prediction and public availability. Given that many prior studies suffer from dataset inconsistencies and reproducibility limitations, we curated an independent test set targeting S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa, ensuring no sequence overlap with the training data of the compared tools. The number of AMPs used for each species is provided in Supplementary Table S7, and the complete sequences used for independent evaluation are provided in Supplementary Data S2.

Figure 4C provides a visual summary of the performance comparison across four evaluation metrics for each bacterium. ANIA consistently outperformed all baseline models, showing both higher correlation with experimental log MIC values and lower prediction errors across all three pathogens. For S. aureus, ANIA improved PCC from 0.2304 (ESKAPEE-Pred) and 0.5486 (esAMPMIC) to 0.6227, while reducing MSE from 0.4016 to 0.2348. Similarly, for E. coli, ANIA attained the highest PCC (0.7046), exceeding esAMPMIC (0.6045) and AMPActiPred (0.4651), and maintained low MAE and MSE values. The most notable improvement was observed for P. aeruginosa, where traditional tools exhibited limited predictive power (PCC < 0.48), yet ANIA achieved a substantial performance gain with a PCC of 0.5902 and the lowest MSE (0.2335).

These results demonstrate ANIA’s superior ability to capture MIC-relevant sequence patterns, particularly under challenging conditions such as those presented by P. aeruginosa. The full numerical results are available in Supplementary Table S8. Collectively, this comparative evaluation reinforces ANIA’s value as a reliable and generalizable deep learning framework for AMP activity prediction and provides details of the ANIA web server in supplementary note 1.6.

sec.title: Discussion and Conclusion
sec.p: The rise of bacterial resistance highlights the need for alternative therapies. AMPs, with broad-spectrum efficacy, offer a promising option. Predicting AMP activity is crucial for their development. Here, we present ANIA, a model predicting AMP MICs for S. aureus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa, meeting the demand for accurate, interpretable tools. The ANIA model integrates spatial features extracted via FCGR with a deep learning architecture. To enhance transparency, we incorporated multiple interpretability techniques—including motif-level composition mapping, Grad-CAM visualizations, correlation mapping, motif frequency analysis, and physicochemical profiling. Comparative assessments demonstrated that ANIA consistently outperformed existing tools such as ESKAPEE-Pred, esAMPMIC, and AMPActiPred, achieving higher correlation coefficients and reduced errors. The most notable improvement was observed in P. aeruginosa, where prior models exhibited limited predictive capacity.

Motif-based analysis identified four key FCGR subregions linked to low MICs, marked by strong Grad-CAM attention and negative correlations. Hydrophobicity mapping showed higher hydrophobicity in these areas aligned with stronger activity, consistent with prior findings on AMP–membrane interactions. To enhance usability, we developed the ANIA web interface, allowing users to input peptide sequences and obtain MIC predictions for three clinically relevant bacterial species. This resource offers a practical tool for evaluating peptide potency and supports rational AMP design.

Despite its strong performance, our study has certain limitations. The dataset, though carefully curated, remains modest in size, which may restrict model generalizability. Moreover, while FCGR-based encoding effectively captures spatial features, exploring alternative representations—including structure-informed or evolutionary embeddings, as well as peptide descriptors that account for post-translational modifications—may offer further improvements [54–56]. Future research should aim to expand the dataset, incorporate descriptors and extend prediction to antiviral or anticancer activity. Moreover, the ANIA framework, which combines CGR-based spatial encoding with Inception-Attention modeling, is conceptually generalizable to other peptide-related prediction tasks, such as toxicity or hemolytic activity forecasting. In conclusion, ANIA provides a robust, interpretable MIC prediction framework, supporting peptide discovery and advancing strategies against antimicrobial resistance.

list-item.p: Antimicrobial resistance necessitates the development of predictive tools for evaluating peptide efficacy beyond conventional classification tasks.
ANIA is a deep learning framework that integrates CGR and a hybrid Inception–Transformer architecture to predict MIC values of AMPs.
Benchmark comparisons with existing tools demonstrate that ANIA consistently outperforms baseline models across three clinically relevant bacteria, especially P. aeruginosa.
Motif-level interpretability analyses identify biologically meaningful FCGR subregions, linking sequence motifs and physicochemical properties to antimicrobial potency.
A publicly available ANIA web server enables MIC prediction from user-submitted AMP sequences, facilitating rational peptide design and translational applications.
